newsitem.title: USA: Nippon Cargo mulls new U.S. gateways.
newsitem.headline: Nippon Cargo mulls new U.S. gateways.

text.p: After selecting Anchorage last month as one of its three new gateways, other U.S. airports are ardently wooing Nippon Cargo Airlines in an attempt to win one of its two remaining gateway slots, a Nippon executive told Reuters.

"They are pursuing us aggressively. We have visited quite a few places and received a lot of materials," Peter Diefenbach, New York-based assistant director of sales and marketing for Nippon Cargo Airlines, said in an interview. Under agreements between Japan and the U.S. government, Nippon is allowed to fly into three new U.S. cities.
"We want to be in the right place at the right time," Diefenbach said.
The decision probably will not be made until the first quarter of 1998. "We are short airplanes. We have seven now and an eighth will be converted soon," Diefenbach said.
Currently Nippon Cargo flies into New York, Chicago, San Francisco and Los Angeles in the U.S.. These cities account for about 78 percent of Asian exports in the U.S., Diefenbach said.
"We can always change these (four) cities too," he said.

Nippon has a detailed list of criteria with which it is trying to evaluate the best two choices. Diefenbach said the ideal airport would be situated in a market with local production of an air-eligible commodity and have additional cargo potential within a 400 mile radius.
Nippon wants to see demand for air both inbound and outbound and requires a strong freight forwarding network.
As to the specifics of the airport, Diefenbach wants to have adequate cargo facilities and full nighttime operations.

The facility has to be able to handle all types of special cargo such as perishables, live animals, dangerous and high value goods and outsized cargo. "We are a large carrier of perishables and live animals," he said.
Airport fees must be reasonable, and the airport must have good support services such as security and catering and regulatory services such as U.S. Customs and Department of Agriculture.
Miami International Airport has made no secret of its interest in Nippon Cargo and is emphasizing its stranglehold position as the cargo gateways to the huge and growing Latin American market.

The interest grabbing Nippon Cargo is a little surprising to Diefenbach. "I will say this. I have been in the cargo business a long time and it is only in the last three or four years I have seen much (airport) interest in cargo carriers."
